doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Wilbert Baranco and the 1946 Black & White date with Dizzy Gillespie
summary: Baranco calls him to Los Angeles for a recording with Gillespie, McGhee, Mingus and others; he never heard the results.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Yes. In the Navy. And also in the mid-forties after the war Wilbert went to Los Angeles. See because he had lived there before and he knew all the musicians down there. They knew all the guys in the union. Curtis Mosby, you’ll see his name in the annals, big band annals, Wilbert had been on the road with him, oh back in I guess the early thirties. Anyhow Wilbert went to Los Angeles. And as I said not only was he a fine pianist but he was a fine arranger. So Wilbert, he got in down there. He was working, he had a gig — a noontime gig, pianist/single; a cocktail session gig; and an evening gig, single; and then he was arranging. He was writing. He was selling his arrangements and he got a recording contract with Black & White. He got a date. And this is 1946. And he called me up from Los Angeles and asked me to come down there and do that date with him. So I hustled myself down to Los Angeles. I was working at the Band Box in Menlo Park at the time with Buddy Collette and Ernie Royal and a fella named Jimmy Shorter, a pianist, we had a quartet. So I got Bobby Alsbin to sub for me and I went down to Los Angeles. And we had to go out to the studio, out in Santa Monica. And I went to the studio. And here you have Dizzy Gillespie, Howard McGhee, Carl George, and another fella, I can’t remember the fourth trumpet player. Then the trombones, I can’t remember their names. Willie Smith on lead alto. Lucky Thompson on tenor. Then I can’t remember the rest of the saxophone section. Mingus on the bass. And there I am sitting up there. And so we did several tunes for Black & White. And I understand now that some company in England I guess bought up the masters. And someone told me that they saw in one of the magazines this Wilbert Baranco recording with Dizzy on it, and of course I never got copies, never even heard them.
Wouldn’t that be interesting now to hear it.
